summary: Wilde's letters to the journalist Rowland Strong in 1898, on how The Ballad had done and what a good review was worth to him.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote: I send you a copy of my Ballad, which I hope you will accept with the author's compliments … The copy is of the first edition, which, I am glad to say, has now some interest for the bibliophile, and fetches a high price in London: it was exhausted on the day of issue. The poem has been a great success, I am glad to say, and the Press has not boycotted it after all.
sources.context: Wilde to Rowland Strong, Tuesday [February-March 1898], Hôtel de Nice (TS Clark). The editors note the text is supported by an entry in a 1911 bookseller's catalogue. The elision is the editors' own, marking a cut in their copy-text rather than one made here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own account of how The Ballad had done, sent to a journalist.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1073. The volume heads this letter 'TS Clark' - a TYPESCRIPT, not Wilde's hand. Nothing in it can settle emphasis: whoever typed it had already read the underlining.

manuscript.repository: William Andrews Clark Memorial Library, UCLA

sources.quote:
I cannot tell you what pleasure your letter gave me, I wish my poem had fallen into your hands for review. Though I have had some most sympathetic and intellectual criticisms, nothing that has been said about The Ballad has touched me, or encouraged me, as much as your letter … In the meanwhile, have you any money to spare? If you have it would be very kind of you if you would lend me fifty francs. I am quite sans le sou, and awaiting money from my absurd publisher …

OSCAR WILDE
sources.context: Wilde to Rowland Strong, [February-March 1898], Hôtel de Nice (TS Clark). The elisions are the editors'. The join is the point: the warmest sentence in the letter and the request for fifty francs are two paragraphs apart, and by 1898 the two things travel together in almost every letter Wilde writes.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What a good review was worth to him, and what he needed in the same breath.

sources.context: Paris is believed to be a place of the connection - Strong was a Paris-based journalist - but no source in this record names the city: the two cited letters are both written from the Hotel de Nice (February-March 1898).
sources.supports: Would settle Paris as a place of the connection: the volume's Strong index entry, read at the page.
